strengths: Novel and well-motivated perspective shift from user-oriented to problem-oriented optimization pairs with clear intuitive appeal and practical justification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple Code LLMs (CodeLLama, DeepSeek-Coder) with both BEST@1 and BEST@8 strategies
Strong empirical evidence that problem-oriented pairs focus on global algorithmic optimizations (78-84%) vs. local optimizations (27-32%) in user-oriented pairs
Rigorous evaluation methodology using gem5 CPU simulator for deterministic, reproducible execution time measurements
Detailed error analysis and sensitivity studies (merge weights, optimization categorization) providing actionable insights
Substantial empirical improvements: optimization ratio increases from 51.76% to 76.65% and speedup from 2.65× to 5.09×
Clear contribution of PIE-Problem dataset and commitment to reproducibility through public code/data release
weaknesses: Significant correctness degradation under PIE-Problem training (37-72% BEST@1, 45-79% BEST@8) vs. PIE-User (31-59%, 77-91%) with ~66% test case failures limiting practical applicability
Critical design choice (90% relative time improvement threshold) lacks principled justification; no ablation studies on threshold sensitivity despite its major impact on dataset composition
Substantial dataset reduction (14,051 vs. 56,086 pairs; 336 vs. 1,135 unique problems) raises generalization concerns despite quality>quantity argument
Model merging approach feels post-hoc, addressing symptoms rather than root causes of correctness issues; mechanism for why weight averaging improves robustness is inadequately explained
Limited scope: only time optimization for C++ competitive programming code; generalization to other languages, problem domains, and optimization objectives unclear
Incomplete comparisons: missing baselines with other code optimization approaches, program repair techniques, and comparison with compiler-only optimizations
Model merging improvements in Table 3 are inconsistent for correctness metric, contradicting claim that merging 'retains quality while providing benefits'
Only 100 human annotations vs. 1,000 GPT-4 annotations for optimization type categorization; small human sample weakens analysis
Curriculum learning degrades performance with only speculative explanation; insufficient analysis of why intermediate merge weights (λ∈[0.5,0.8]) outperform pure PIE-Problem
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals; lack of analysis on how performance scales with program size and complexity
Limited discussion of when user-oriented approach might be preferable; insufficient treatment of safety concerns and deployment challenges with 70% correctness rates

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core observation: The intuitive insight that diverse programmers bring different perspectives, enabling discovery of more innovative algorithms, is convincingly illustrated (especially Figure 2)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The paper evaluates multiple Code LLMs (CodeLlama 7B/13B/34B, DeepSeek-Coder 7B/33B) with multiple configurations (BEST@1 and BEST@8), showing consistent improvements with PIE-Problem
Reproducibility emphasis: Use of gem5 CPU simulator for deterministic execution timing, promise to release dataset/code/scripts, and detailed training parameters in appendix are commendable

Thorough analysis and presentation: Error analysis (Table 4), merge weight analysis (Figure 5), optimization type categorization, and additional examples in appendices demonstrate careful investigation
Substantial empirical improvements: Reported gains from 51.76% to 76.65% in optimization ratio and 2.65× to 5.09× speedup with model merging are notable
weaknesses: Unfair dataset comparison: PIE-Problem uses 90% relative improvement threshold vs. 10% for PIE-User, resulting in 14,051 pairs vs. 56,086 pairs and only 336 unique problems vs. 1,135. This makes it impossible to isolate whether improvements come from the perspective shift or simply from higher-quality, higher-effort training data. Critical missing ablation: what happens when comparing PIE-User pairs that also exceed 90% improvement?

Limited novelty: The core contribution is data curation/reconstruction rather than methodological innovation. No new training techniques, optimization algorithms, or architectural improvements are proposed—only a different way to pair existing code samples

Critical correctness problem undermines practical utility: Correctness drops dramatically under PIE-Problem (37.41% for DeepSeek 33B BEST@1 vs. 59.49% for PIE-User). The gap between %OPT (36.64%) and Correct (37.41%) is negligible, suggesting generated optimizations are mostly incorrect. Real deployment requires >>95% correctness; this work achieves ~73-79% at best

Model merging as a patch, not a principled solution: Combining models trained on opposite optimization directions (PIE-User: conservative, PIE-Problem: aggressive) lacks theoretical justification. The paper provides only empirical validation without explaining why this works. This suggests PIE-Problem has fundamental limitations that aren't properly addressed

Shallow analysis of categorization reliability: Figure 3 shows discrepancies between GPT-4 (83.7% global) and human (78.0% global) classifications for PIE-Problem. No inter-annotator agreement metrics, and the brief dismissal ('GPT-4 tends to classify... with large changes') questions whether the optimization type categorization is meaningful

Missing critical ablations: (1) No systematic study of the 90% threshold—what if it were 70%, 50%? (2) No comparison using equal numbers of pairs from both datasets. (3) No analysis of sensitivity to BEST@k value. (4) No ablation on training epochs (why only 2?)

Weak experimental baselines: Comparisons limited to prompt-based methods (Instruct, CoT). Prior work on code optimization (DeepPERF, compiler optimization methods) mentioned but not empirically compared against

Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing. Results appear to be single runs with unknown variance. Reproducibility across different random seeds is unclear

Curriculum learning failure unexplained: The paper tries curriculum learning but it underperforms (Table 3). The post-hoc explanation is speculative and suggests incomplete understanding of why the approach fails

Limited generalizability: Scope restricted to (1) C++ only, (2) competitive programming only, (3) time optimization only (not memory/space), (4) synthetic problems. Results may not transfer to production code, other languages, or different optimization objectives

Unclear why PIE-Problem has low correctness: If PIE-Problem pairs represent truly global algorithmic improvements and cleaner training signal, why does correctness degrade so severely? This suggests the problem-oriented perspective may have inherent limitations for LLMs that aren't explored

Arbitrary design choices lack justification: The 10% speedup threshold for %OPT metric, gem5 simulator representativeness vs. actual hardware, and choice of LoRA configuration (rank=8, specific targets) are presented without ablation or justification

strengths: Well-motivated insight: The core observation that user-oriented optimization pairs limit LLMs to local improvements due to single programmer's thought patterns is compelling and grounded in software engineering practices; problem-oriented pairs effectively capture algorithmic innovation

Rigorous experimental methodology: Uses gem5 CPU simulator for deterministic execution measurement (gold standard); comprehensive evaluation across 5 Code LLM variants; appropriate metrics (%OPT, SPEEDUP, Correctness); proper BEST@k sampling with temperature control

Careful dataset construction: 90% speedup threshold well-justified for defining 'global' optimization; manual analysis by GPT-4 and humans validates 83.7% global optimizations in PIE-Problem vs 32% in PIE-User; strict train/val/test split integrity

Effective bottleneck analysis and resolution: Clear identification that correctness is the performance bottleneck; thoughtful application of model merging with thorough merge weight analysis (Figure 5); proper comparison with Self-Correct and Curriculum Learning baselines

Strong empirical results: Consistent improvements across model scales; best model achieves 71.03% %OPT (BEST@8), substantial speedup gains from 2.65× to 5.09×; results hold across different parameter sizes

Excellent presentation and clarity: Well-written with intuitive visualizations; Figures 1-3 effectively convey concepts; detailed code examples (Figures 2, 8-10) strongly support claims; compelling narrative
Good reproducibility: Commitment to release dataset, code, and evaluation scripts; detailed training parameters in appendices; deterministic evaluation methodology enables reproduction
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution is a dataset perspective shift rather than novel methods; model merging techniques (Merge-Linear, Slerp) are existing approaches; LoRA fine-tuning is standard; contribution is incremental despite useful practical value

Insufficient analysis of dataset size effects: 75% reduction in training data (336 problems, 14,051 pairs vs 1,135 problems, 56,086); lacks ablation studies examining whether improvements stem from data quality vs. perspective shift vs. size reduction; missing sensitivity analysis on the 90% speedup threshold choice

Incomplete baseline comparisons: No direct comparison with original Shypula et al. (2024) PIE paper results; limited comparison with other code optimization approaches; prompt-based methods perform surprisingly poorly but unclear if due to suboptimal prompting or fundamental limitations

Statistical rigor concerns: No confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing reported; manual optimization categorization limited to 100 human samples; unclear whether experiments use single or multiple random seeds; variance across runs not reported

Persistent correctness bottleneck: Even best model (DeepSeek-Coder 33B) achieves only 78.76% correctness; Table 4 shows 66% of failures due to functional incorrectness; limits practical applicability; program repair techniques only briefly mentioned without deep exploration

Narrow scope and generalization: Limited to time complexity optimization (not memory, energy); restricted to C++ competitive programming; no evaluation on real-world production code or other languages; unclear how well insights transfer beyond competitive programming domain

Incomplete analysis of model performance variance: DeepSeek-Coder 7B outperforms CodeLlama 34B (size-inverse relationship); explanation attributing to 'code semantic understanding' is speculative without deeper investigation

Curriculum learning unexpectedly underperforms: Degrades performance compared to PIE-Problem alone; explanation that optimization spaces are 'entirely different' lacks theoretical support; suggests potential brittleness

Missing critical ablations: No threshold sensitivity analysis; no investigation of different speedup thresholds (50%, 75%); no ablation on BEST@k values; no analysis of actual improvement threshold needed to influence model behavior

strengths: Clear problem motivation with well-articulated limitations of user-oriented approach and intuitive examples showing advantages of diverse solutions
Comprehensive multi-faceted analysis (structural via CFGs, semantic via embeddings, human+LLM sampling) rigorously comparing problem-oriented vs user-oriented perspectives
Strong consistent empirical results across multiple LLM architectures with ~90% relative improvement in optimization ratio (31.24%→58.89%) and compelling data efficiency finding (30% PCO > full PIE)
Practical and clever anchor verification mechanism that leverages guaranteed-correct slow code as test anchor, with concrete case studies demonstrating real benefits
Good reproducibility with publicly available code, detailed training parameters, hyperparameters, and prompts in appendices
weaknesses: Problem-oriented perspective has limited conceptual novelty—essentially a data curation strategy where sorting by runtime and pairing solutions is relatively straightforward; the core insight that diverse solutions help is intuitive

Narrow experimental scope limited to competitive programming (AtCoder, C++ only) with small test set (41 problems, 978 pairs); generalization to real-world code, different languages, and other domains remains unclear

Unresolved correctness-optimization trade-off: Finding 1 shows CORRECT declines under BEST@8 for PCO despite better optimization; even after anchor verification, correctness plateaus at ~74.54%, inadequate for critical systems

PCO construction uses 'top speedup' selection to maintain fair pair count, potentially introducing bias toward particular optimization patterns; unclear whether improvements stem from diversity or preferential selection of better pairs; no ablation on selection criterion

Anchor verification has limited novelty (combines existing techniques) and circular limitations: only catches bugs in slow code's test paths; edge cases outside slow code's behavior space are missed; no analysis of LLM-generated test input quality or multi-iteration exploration

Incomplete baseline comparisons: Self-debugging and direct test generation only introduced in Section 4.2; no comparison with traditional compilers or other optimization approaches; limited exploration of sensitivity to construction choices via ablations
Missing statistical analysis: no confidence intervals, significance testing, or error bars despite potential variance; with 41 test problems, statistical rigor would strengthen claims

Practical deployment concerns not addressed: computational cost of BEST@8 not discussed; users typically want single output; scalability to large codebases unclear; anchor verification iterations capped at 1 without justification

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem with intuitive examples demonstrating limitations of user-oriented optimization pairs
Comprehensive multi-dimensional analysis (structural, semantic, and human/LLM sampling) providing insights into dataset differences
Strong and consistent empirical improvements across multiple LLM architectures and sizes
Practical anchor verification mechanism that cleverly leverages the correct slow code as a test anchor
Data efficiency analysis demonstrating that 30% of PCO pairs match full PIE performance
Detailed case studies providing concrete examples of the approach in practice
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: Problem-oriented perspective is essentially a dataset re-ordering strategy rather than a novel technical contribution
Dataset construction fairness concerns: PCO limited to 78K pairs via 'top speedup' selection introduces selection bias; no justification for this strategy or comparison against alternative selections
Causality unclear: Improvements could stem from problem diversity, selection bias toward harder examples, or the ordering itself; paper doesn't isolate these factors
Anchor verification confounds results: Method is orthogonal to PCO and adds ~12% CORRECT gain; unclear how much improvement comes from PCO vs. verification; only briefly evaluated on PIE in appendix
Weak baselines for anchor verification: Self-Debugging and Direct Test Generation were not designed for code optimization; max iteration set to 1 is arbitrary and under-explores iterative gains
Lacks statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or per-problem analysis; test set small (978 pairs, 41 problems); no formal statistical comparison between methods

Narrow scope limiting generalization: Only time optimization (not memory); only C/C++ competitive programming; generalization to real-world code unclear; results on gem5 simulator may not transfer to real hardware

Incomplete analysis and missing ablations: Figure 2-4 analysis is somewhat superficial; human annotation limited to 100 pairs; only 1 ablation study (PCO percentage); no analysis of which problems benefit most

Missing key experiments: No ablation on PCO selection strategy; no comparison of all available PCO pairs vs. top-speedup filtered subset; no consistent application of anchor verification to PIE baseline
Finding 1 (CORRECT decline at BEST@8) suggests PCO encourages risky changes, but issue is glossed over rather than investigated

strengths: Clear problem identification and well-motivated solution: Identifies real limitation in user-oriented optimization pairs and proposes practical problem-oriented alternative
Significant empirical improvements: 2x improvement in optimization ratio (31.24% → 58.89%), 1.77x improvement in speedup (2.95× → 5.22×), consistent across multiple LLMs
Comprehensive multi-dimensional analysis: Structural (GED), semantic (t-SNE), and human/LLM categorization providing insight into differences between approaches
Thorough experimental evaluation: Tests across 4 LLM families and scales, multiple decoding strategies, data efficiency analysis, proper train/val/test splits
Practical anchor verification mechanism: Clever three-stage approach using functionally correct slow code as test anchor, addresses real correctness-efficiency trade-off
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: Clear writing, detailed appendices with prompts/training details, case studies, code availability promised
Data efficiency insight: Shows 30% of PCO pairs surpass full PIE, indicating superior data efficiency of problem-oriented approach
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Problem-oriented perspective is straightforward reordering of pairs by runtime; combining multi-source solutions is intuitive rather than innovative
Domain-specific scope: Limited to competitive programming (CodeNet), C/C++ code, time-only optimization; generalization to production code, web dev, systems programming unclear
Insufficient analysis of correctness-optimization trade-off: Finding 1 notes CORRECT declines under BEST@8 on PCO but root causes not analyzed; arbitrary choice of max iteration=1 unexplained
Weak anchor verification baselines: Direct test generation is somewhat strawman-ish; no comparison with domain-specific test generation tools or formal verification methods
Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance analysis; results appear to be single runs; BEST@k computational cost not discussed
No failure mode analysis: Missing discussion of when/why methods fail, examples of optimization failures anchor verification cannot fix, or analysis of test case generation quality
Limited baseline comparisons: Only compared against PIE; could simple reordering of PIE pairs achieve similar gains? Missing ablation on data construction specifics
Test case generation underspecified: Stage 1 generates only 3 test cases with no analysis of coverage adequacy or discussion of failure cases when LLM cannot explain code

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation with clear distinction between user-oriented and problem-oriented perspectives, grounded in real-world collaborative optimization practices
Comprehensive multi-dimensional analysis including structural (GED), semantic (embeddings), and human sampling analysis that rigorously validates the effectiveness of the perspective shift

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple LLM models (DeepSeek, GPT-4, CodeLLaMA, Qwen), with appropriate baselines and thorough ablation studies (GED-stratified subsets, PCO-Random vs. PCO-Top-Speedup)
Practical anchor verification framework that cleverly exploits code optimization's unique property (slow code is functionally correct), with clear three-stage design and concrete case studies
Strong and consistent empirical results (31.24% → 58.90% → 71.06% optimization rate; 2.95× → 5.22× → 6.08× speedup) with data efficiency benefits (30% PCO data exceeds 100% PIE)
Rigorous hardware validation (Pearson correlation 0.89 with simulations) and cross-language validation (Python) demonstrating broad applicability
Excellent reproducibility with extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, failure analysis (Table 7), and prompts provided in appendices
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: problem-oriented perspective is conceptually straightforward (reorder by runtime), and anchor verification largely adapts existing test-case feedback mechanisms; both read as engineering rather than algorithmic contributions

Critical unresolved correctness issue: final correctness reaches only 74.54% with ~53% of failures being semantic errors (Table 7); anchor verification incrementally improves but doesn't address fundamental semantic understanding limitations, limiting practical deployment viability

Narrow evaluation scope restricted to competitive programming domain (CodeNet) with unclear transferability to industrial codebases; focuses solely on execution time optimization while ignoring memory, energy, and other practical concerns; small test set (41 problems, 978 pairs)

Methodological concern: PCO dataset uses top-speedup selection while PIE uses all sequential pairs, creating potentially unfair comparison; though Appendix H addresses this, the main paper doesn't adequately discuss this design choice

Practical cost limitations inadequately addressed: BEST@8 (used for best results) requires 8× inference cost; anchor verification adds 7-15s overhead per sample (Table 11); 48 GPU hours for fine-tuning not contextualized with cost-benefit analysis

Anchor verification framework assumptions and limitations: assumes slow reference code availability, shows diminishing returns beyond single iteration (Table 4), admits 'intolerable slow code' scenarios requiring manual workarounds (Section L), but these limitations only discussed in appendices

Limited baseline comparisons: no comparison with DeepPerf, evolutionary computation methods, or other code optimization approaches; missing statistical significance tests and confidence intervals; human analysis limited to 100 samples

Speculative generalizability claims: discussion of real-world applications to open-source projects (Section 4) lacks concrete evidence; Python shows higher correctness (89.27% vs 61.55%) but attribution to language properties vs. LLM bias unexplored; scalability to large programs unknown

strengths: Addresses an underexplored and practical problem (LLM-based code optimization) with clear motivation for both proposed ideas
Comprehensive multi-dimensional experimental evaluation including structural analysis (GED), semantic analysis (t-SNE), human annotation, cross-language validation (Python), and hardware validation
Strong empirical results across multiple LLM architectures (58.90% %OPT vs. 31.24% baseline, 5.22× speedup)
Practical anchor verification framework cleverly exploits task structure by using slow-but-correct code as ground truth for test case generation
Thorough ablation studies and appendices with implementation details, prompts, failure analysis, and case studies supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation of the problem-oriented vs. user-oriented distinction with intuitive motivation
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: problem-oriented perspective is fundamentally a data construction strategy (aggregate by problem rather than user); anchor verification combines standard test generation with iterative refinement—both are existing techniques

Dataset comparison is confounded: PCO uses 'top speedup' pair selection while maintaining equal counts to PIE. Appendix H shows PCO-Random (random selection) also beats PIE (49.55% vs 26.96% %OPT), undermining claims that 'perspective drives gains' vs. selection strategy. Fair comparison requires controlling for selection criteria

Evaluation metrics mask practical concerns: assigning 1.0× speedup to failures obscures ~26-38% failure rate; %OPT metric conflates correctness and speed; Finding 1 shows CORRECT degrades at BEST@8 for PCO (83.03% vs 87.95% for PIE), suggesting the method sacrifices correctness for speedup—the opposite of addressing 'optimization tax'

Incomplete solution to central problem: anchor verification achieves only 74.54% correctness, meaning ~1 in 4 optimizations fail. Paper acknowledges 'zero-correctness-loss remains open challenge' but positions work as addressing this. Table 7 shows 53% of failures are semantic errors with no proposed solution

Generalizability not demonstrated: experiments limited to CodeNet competitive programming (well-defined I/O, time as sole objective, small programs with clear logic). Real-world code differs fundamentally. Section 4 claims generalization to 'complex scenarios' but provides no concrete evidence—discussion is speculative

Limited baseline comparisons: only compares PCO vs PIE fine-tuning; no comparison to other code optimization methods (GEVO, DeepPerf, etc.) mentioned in related work. Prompting baselines (CoT: 31.92% %OPT) confirm fine-tuning is necessary but don't isolate what makes method effective

Insufficient analysis of causation: why does diversity help? GED analysis shows higher distances but higher GED ≠ better signal (could be noise). t-SNE visualization is qualitative; quantitative clustering metrics missing. Learning edit patterns (Appendix O) supported by single case study—anecdotal
No statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance testing. Human evaluation on only 100 samples. Single runs reported per model

Missing ablations: no study of anchor verification components independently (Stage 1 alone? without filtering?); fixed at 3 test cases without justification; iteration count guidance absent; prompt design unjustified

strengths: Well-motivated problem-oriented perspective with rigorous multi-dimensional validation (structural GED analysis, semantic embeddings, human evaluation)
Significant and consistent improvements across multiple LLM models/scales (31.24%→58.90% %OPT, 2.95×→5.22× SPEEDUP) with strong data efficiency (30% PCO achieves better results than full PIE)
Thorough experimental evaluation including ablations (Appendix H), learning edit patterns analysis, hardware validation, and cross-language validation
Practical anchor verification framework leveraging unique domain property (slow-but-correct code) with measurable improvements over baselines
Excellent reproducibility with detailed training configs, hyperparameters, prompts, and code compilation details documented
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: problem-oriented reorganization is straightforward engineering; anchor verification combines established techniques (execution feedback + ground-truth verification)

Scope and generalization concerns: evaluation restricted to time optimization on competitive programming; unclear transfer to industrial codebases, different problem types, or other optimization objectives; training data overlap with LLM pretraining data

Fundamental anchor verification limitations: 53% of remaining failures are semantic errors unsolved by framework (Table 7); 'optimization tax' term misleading—it's an inherent tradeoff, not fixable bug
Data scarcity claim insufficiently justified: mathematically reorganizing existing data rather than collecting new data; missing comparison with collecting more user-oriented pairs

Evaluation limitations: small test set (41 problems), no statistical significance tests, arbitrary thresholds, CORRECT metric declines at BEST@8 in PCO suggesting unresolved accuracy-efficiency tradeoff
